sections.h1: Wayfinding and Directional Signs in New York City for Buildings
sections.lead_html:
A good sign answers where to turn before a visitor has to ask.

Vision Graphics designs and makes wayfinding and directional signs for NYC offices, schools, and multi-tenant buildings, as part of our interior signs in NYC range. We plan the route with you and manage installation through licensed partners.

sections.html:
A directional sign points the way at a single decision point, such as a corridor junction. Wayfinding is the whole system: destination names, numbering, sign types, and the route between them.

Directional signs are one part of it, so plan the system first and then place each sign where a visitor must choose.

Wayfinding design starts with the route. Wayfinding systems keep names, arrows, and numbering consistent from the entrance to the door.

sections.h2: The Four Types of Wayfinding Signs
sections.html:
Most buildings need all four types working together. The table shows what each does and which rules apply.

Sign typeWhat it doesExamplesRules to know
IdentificationConfirms arrival at a room, suite, or floorRoom, suite, and floor signs. See door signs in NYC, ADA signs in NYC, and restroom signs in NYC.Permanent room signs need raised characters and Braille, where provided, under the ADA Standards.
DirectionalPoints the way at a decisionWall, overhead, flag, and floor signs with arrowsThe ADA Standards ask for visual criteria only.
InformationalShows what is nearby and where things areDirectories, hours, and maps. See directory signs in NYC.Visual criteria apply to informational signs. Building directories are exempt under the ADA Standards.
RegulatorySets rules or safety informationAccess rules and safety noticesNYC life-safety rules and approved materials may apply. Our team confirms what we supply.

These notes describe the standards. Your building or design professional confirms what applies, and our team can discuss specifications.

sections.intro_html: Indoor directional signs in NYC come in several formats, and each suits a different sightline. Custom directional signs can match your building's finishes, so match the format to the corridor, the ceiling, and the pace of foot traffic.

items.title: Wall-Mounted Directional Signs
items.html: Directional signs with arrows sit at corridor junctions and lobby decision points. In NYC buildings, directional wall signs work at a height people can read while walking.

items.title: Projecting and Flag Signs
items.html: A flag sign stands out from the wall so people see it down a corridor. Under the ADA Standards, wall-mounted objects between 27 and 80 inches may project only 4 inches.

items.title: Overhead Signs
items.html: Overhead directional signage helps in open lobbies and wide corridors where wall signs are hidden. The ADA Standards call for at least 80 inches of clearance below them.

items.title: Floor Graphics
items.html: Floor graphics guide people through open areas and queues. See floor graphics in NYC for options.

items.title: Temporary Route Signs
items.html: Temporary route signs direct events, moves, and short-term changes. Plan the material and the removal around the display dates.

sections.h2: Planning a Wayfinding System for an NYC Building
sections.intro_html: A wayfinding signage plan starts with the route and ends with a sign schedule. These five steps keep the plan consistent from the entrance to the door.

items.title: Walk the Route as a First-Time Visitor
items.html: Trace the journey from each entrance to the main destinations and note each unclear turn. Ask someone who does not know the building to try it too.

items.title: Name Each Destination Once
items.html: Use one name for each room, department, and tenant on all signs. Two labels for one place send visitors the wrong way.

items.title: Plan Floor and Suite Numbering
items.html: Floor and suite numbers need a logical order that signs and directories repeat. Share your numbering plan early so the sign schedule matches it.

items.title: Plan for Tenant Changes
items.html: List what changes often, such as tenant names and meeting room names. Updateable components may suit those, and fixed panels suit stable destinations.

items.title: Review Accessibility Early
items.html: Ask your design professional which ADA Standards apply, then share the specification with us. Directional signs need visual criteria, and permanent room signs need raised characters and Braille.

sections.h2: Exit and Safety Signs in NYC
sections.intro_html: Visitor wayfinding and life-safety signs do different jobs. NYC rules cover exit and egress markings, and they may change.

items.title: Exit Path Markings
items.html: High-rise office buildings may need photoluminescent exit path markings in approved materials under Local Law 26 of 2004. These markings help people find the way out when lighting fails.

items.title: Approved Materials
items.html: NYC lists approved products, and shipments need manufacturer certification. The building owner handles the filings.

items.title: What We Supply
items.html: Our team confirms which safety signs we supply for your building. Send your building's exit sign requirements early so we can plan visitor wayfinding and safety signs together.

sections.intro_html: Choose materials by what changes. Permanent destinations suit fixed panels, and changing names suit updateable components.

items.title: Fixed Panels
items.html: Acrylic, aluminum, and photopolymer panels suit stable destinations such as stairs and main corridors. They keep a consistent look across a building.

items.title: Updateable Components
items.html: Updateable components let you change a name without replacing a whole sign. Our team confirms the options and how replacements are ordered.

items.title: Finish and Brand Match
items.html: Finish and color should match your building's standards across all signs. Send brand guidelines or photos of existing signs so new signs sit beside them.

sections.intro_html: Each kind of building has its own routes and its own changes.

items.title: Offices
items.html: Offices need clear routes from reception to meeting rooms and departments. See signs for offices and properties.

items.title: Multi-Tenant Buildings
items.html: Lobby wayfinding signs in NYC multi-tenant buildings start the route at the door. Tenant names change often, so see lobby signs in NYC and office signs in NYC.

items.title: Schools
items.html: Schools need routes for visitors, families, and staff across wings and floors. Plan for room and department changes. Learn more about school signs.

items.title: Healthcare
items.html: Healthcare sites need calm, readable routes from the entrance to waiting areas and exam rooms. Large letters and consistent names help patients and visitors.

items.title: Coworking Spaces
items.html: Coworking spaces often change membership and room layouts. Updateable signs and a clear naming plan keep routes readable.

items.title: Phased Installs

items.title: Building Approval and Insurance
items.html: Interior signs may require approval from building management or the landlord, and we can prepare the drawings they request. We can provide a certificate of insurance upon request, and our team will confirm your building's requirements.

items.q: How much do wayfinding signs cost for an office floor or building?
items.a_html: Cost depends on the number of decision points, sign types, and sizes. Planning ranges are about $50 to $150 for standard indoor directional and identification signs and $100 to $250 for corridor directionals. Installation scope is stated in your quote, and your quote replaces these ranges.

items.q: Are your room and suite signs ADA compliant?
items.a_html: The ADA Standards set the rules for these signs. Permanent room signs need raised characters and Braille where they are provided, and directional signs need visual criteria. Your building or design professional confirms what applies, and our team discusses specifications with you.

items.q: Can you match our existing signs or brand standards?
items.a_html: Often yes. Send photos of your existing signs and any brand or sign standards, and our team confirms how closely we can match finish, color, and style. We also show new signs on a drawing before anything is made.

items.q: Can you install in phases while the building is occupied?
items.a_html: Phasing depends on your building, and our team confirms the plan. Tell us your floors, move dates, and building rules, and we schedule the work around them. After-hours work can add labor charges, which we confirm in your quote.

items.q: Do you work after hours for building management?
items.a_html: Yes. We schedule installs around your building's rules, including evenings, weekends, and freight elevator windows. After-hours work can add labor charges, and we confirm them in your quote. Licensed installation partners handle the installation, and our project lead manages the schedule.

items.q: How many directional signs does a building need?
items.a_html: There is no fixed number. Map the route first, then place a directional sign at each decision point and an identification sign at each destination. Consistent names matter more than the count, so share your floor plan and destination list, and we plan the locations with you.

items.q: Are exit signs part of a wayfinding system?
items.a_html: Exit signs follow NYC life-safety rules and are planned separately from visitor wayfinding. High-rise office buildings may need photoluminescent exit path markings in approved materials under Local Law 26 of 2004. Our team confirms which safety signs we supply for your building.

items.q: Can you update signs when tenants change?
items.a_html: Often, with updateable components. They let you change a tenant or room name without replacing the whole sign. Our team confirms the options for your building and how to order replacements. Tell us which names change most, so we plan those signs first.

items.q: What do you need from us to start a wayfinding project?
items.a_html: Send floor plans, a list of destination names, and photos of entrances, corridors, and existing signs. Add quantities if you know them, plus brand guidance, a target date, and the property contact. A floor plan helps even if sign locations are not final.
